title: Chapter XLIX

teacherSummary.text: Mr. Gardiner writes that Lydia and Wickham have been found and will marry on modest terms. Mr. Bennet suspects Gardiner paid a great deal. Mrs. Bennet is overjoyed.

vocabulary.context: Upon this information, they instantly passed through the hall once more, and ran across the lawn after their father, who was deliberately pursuing his way towards a small wood on one side of the paddock.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “paddock”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A fine, thin, and white fabric made of flax or linen
vocabulary.context: She was then proceeding to all the particulars of calico, muslin, and cambric, and would shortly have dictated some very plentiful orders, had not Jane, though with some difficulty, persuaded her to wait, till her father was at leisure to be consulted.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cambric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To agree in opinion or sentiment
vocabulary.context: His consenting to marry her is a proof, I will believe, that he is come to a right way of thinking.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “consent”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + sent (Latin sentire, "to feel"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Their taking her home, and affording her their personal protection and countenance, is such a sacrifice to her advantage as years of gratitude cannot enough acknowledge.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “afford”: af- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: She was disturbed by no fear for her felicity, nor humbled by any remembrance of her misconduct.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “humble”: hum (Latin humus, "earth" / homo, "human"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: An English silver coin of the value of six pennies
vocabulary.context: Gardiner has done for them, because Wickham has not sixpence of his own.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sixpence”: -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (Law) The transfer of possession of personal property from a debtor to a creditor as security for a debt or engagement
vocabulary.context: We are persuaded that he has pledged himself to assist Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pledge”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: My dear Jane, I am in such a flutter, that I am sure I can’t write; so I will dictate, and you write for me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “flutter”: flu (Latin fluere, "to flow") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To relieve of a charge, load, or burden
vocabulary.context: The world has been deceived in that respect; and I am happy to say, there will be some little money, even when all his debts are discharged, to settle on my niece, in addition to her own fortune.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “discharge”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To seek the opinion or advice of another
vocabulary.context: She was then proceeding to all the particulars of calico, muslin, and cambric, and would shortly have dictated some very plentiful orders, had not Jane, though with some difficulty, persuaded her to wait, till her father was at leisure to be consulted.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “consult”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Settlements guaranteed income in marriage; paying a man to marry was a way to restore honor.

significance: Mrs. Bennet's joy ironically ignores the shame and cost.
discussionQuestions: Why is Mrs. Bennet's reaction ironic?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLIX,” how does Austen show a costly solution? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XLIX, how does Austen develop the idea of a costly solution? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLIX develops the idea of a costly solution. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XLIX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of a costly solution. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XLIX suggests about a costly solution. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XLIX to complicate the reader's understanding of a costly solution. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a costly solution responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XLIX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a costly solution follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XLIX and its treatment of a costly solution. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XLIX as evidence for a larger claim about a costly solution in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a costly solution. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: To agree in opinion or sentiment
To seek the opinion or advice of another
To relieve of a charge, load, or burden

satQuestions.passage: “That is very true,” said Elizabeth; “though it had not occurred to me before. His debts to be discharged, and something still to remain! Oh! it must be my uncle’s doings! Generous, good man, I am afraid he has distressed himself. A small sum could not do all this.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLIX”?
options: Rejection and the turn to revenge
Injustice and the burden of silence

annotationFocus.label: Plot
annotationFocus.lookFor: key events and the causes linking them
annotationFocus.passage: “That is very true,” said Elizabeth; “though it had not occurred to me before. His debts to be discharged, and something still to remain! Oh! it must be my uncle’s doings! Generous, good man, I am afraid he has distressed himself. A small sum could not do all this.”

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why is Mrs. Bennet's reaction ironic? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are paddock, cambric, consenting, affording, humbled. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Upon this information, they instantly passed through the hall once more, and ran across the lawn after their father, who was deliberately pursuing his way towards a small wood on one side of the paddock.” Webster's says: A toad or frog. Now the word history: “paddock”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “cambric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “consent”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + sent (Latin sentire, "to feel"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Settlements guaranteed income in marriage; paying a man to marry was a way to restore honor. Why does this chapter matter? Mrs. Bennet's joy ironically ignores the shame and cost. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a costly solution.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Irony, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “That is very true,” said Elizabeth; “though it had not occurred to me before. His debts to be discharged, and something still to remain! Oh! it must be my uncle’s doings! Generous, good man, I am afraid he has distressed himself. A small sum could not do all this.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Plot, Irony, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLIX,” how does Austen show a costly solution? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a costly solution, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes a costly solution. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
